units.title: Chapter 1 - Propositional Logic and Set Theory

sections.heading: Propositions and open statements
paragraphs: A proposition (statement) is a declarative sentence with exactly one truth value: true or false. A question, command or exclamation is not a proposition. A sentence containing a variable, such as x + 2 = 5, is an open statement: its truth depends on the value assigned to x. Substitution or quantification can turn an open statement into a proposition.
The universe (domain) specifies the values a variable may take. Always state or identify the domain before deciding whether a quantified claim is true.

sections.heading: Five logical connectives
bullets: Negation ¬p reverses the truth value of p.
Conjunction p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true.
Inclusive disjunction p ∨ q is false only when both p and q are false; it permits both to be true.
Conditional p → q is false only when p is true and q is false. p is the antecedent/hypothesis; q is the consequent/conclusion.
Biconditional p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value.
‘p only if q’ means p → q; q is necessary for p. ‘p if q’ means q → p. ‘p if and only if q’ means both directions hold.

sections.heading: Truth-table method
bullets: For n distinct component propositions, make 2ⁿ rows to cover every assignment of truth values.
Build columns for component statements first, then evaluate inner connectives before outer ones using parentheses.
A tautology is true on every row; a contradiction is false on every row; a contingency is true on some rows and false on others.
Two forms are logically equivalent when their truth values match on every row, or equivalently when their biconditional is a tautology.
For a conditional p → q, remember the single false row (T,F); this is a frequent source of errors.

sections.heading: Useful equivalences
bullets: Double negation: ¬¬p ≡ p.
De Morgan: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q.
Contrapositive: p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. The converse q → p and inverse ¬p → ¬q are not generally equivalent to the original conditional.
Conditional rewrite: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.
Commutative, associative and distributive laws allow rearranging grouped conjunctions and disjunctions without changing truth value.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: Translate a sentence into symbols carefully; check ‘if’, ‘only if’, ‘unless’ and ‘iff’ direction.
Construct a complete truth table and show intermediate columns, especially for nested expressions.
To disprove a universal claim, give a counterexample; to prove an existential claim, give one witness.

sections.heading: Quantifiers
bullets: Universal quantifier ∀x P(x) means P holds for every x in the stated domain. One counterexample makes it false.
Existential quantifier ∃x P(x) means at least one domain element satisfies P. One witness makes it true.
Negations switch quantifiers: ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x); ¬(∃x P(x)) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Negate the predicate as well as changing the quantifier.
Order matters with multiple quantifiers: ∀x∃y P(x,y) may use a different y for each x; ∃y∀x P(x,y) requires one y that works for every x.

sections.heading: Arguments and validity
paragraphs: An argument has premises (hypotheses) intended to imply a conclusion. It is valid if no assignment makes all premises true and the conclusion false. Validity is about logical form, not whether the premises happen to be true.

sections.heading: Common inference rules
bullets: Modus ponens: p → q, p; therefore q.
Modus tollens: p → q, ¬q; therefore ¬p.
Hypothetical syllogism: p → q, q → r; therefore p → r.
Disjunctive syllogism: p ∨ q, ¬p; therefore q.
A truth table tests validity by checking whether any row has all true premises and a false conclusion. If none exists, the argument is valid.

sections.heading: Sets and notation
bullets: A set is a well-defined collection. x ∈ A means x is an element; x ∉ A means it is not. Order and repetition do not change a set.
Sets can be described verbally, by listing elements, by partial listing, or in set-builder form {x ∈ U : condition on x}.
The empty set ∅ has no elements; the universal set U is the domain for a discussion. Distinguish x ∈ A from {x} ⊆ A.
A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B. A = B exactly when each is a subset of the other. A proper subset A ⊂ B is contained in B and is not equal to B.
The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If A has n elements, P(A) has 2ⁿ members and 2ⁿ−1 proper subsets.

sections.heading: Set operations and Venn diagrams
bullets: Union A ∪ B contains elements in A or B or both; intersection A ∩ B contains elements common to both.
Difference A − B contains elements in A but not B. Complement A′ contains elements in U but not A; it depends on the chosen universal set.
Symmetric difference A Δ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A): elements in exactly one of A and B.
Venn diagrams represent the universal set as the rectangle and sets as closed regions. Shade the required regions for unions, intersections, differences and complements.
De Morgan’s set laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. Union/intersection also satisfy commutative, associative and distributive laws.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: For set equality, show both inclusions or list and compare elements when the sets are finite.
Count subsets using 2ⁿ; do not confuse the number of elements in A with the number of subsets.
For a Venn problem, identify the universal set first and keep complement operations relative to it.

units.title: Chapter 2 - The Real and Complex Number System

sections.heading: Number sets and inclusion
bullets: Natural numbers ℕ are counting numbers (check the module’s convention on whether 0 is included); integers ℤ include negatives and zero; rational numbers ℚ are ratios a/b with integers a,b and b ≠ 0; real numbers ℝ include rational and irrational values.
Irrational numbers cannot be written as a ratio of integers; their decimal expansions do not terminate or repeat periodically. Every rational number has a terminating or repeating decimal expansion.
The sets are nested: ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ. Complex numbers ℂ extend the real numbers and include a + bi, where i² = −1.

sections.heading: Properties and closure
bullets: Closure asks whether applying an operation to members of a set always gives a member of that set. For example, ℕ is closed under addition and multiplication but not subtraction or division.
Addition and multiplication on the usual number systems are commutative and associative; multiplication distributes over addition.
An additive identity is 0 and a multiplicative identity is 1. Additive inverses exist in ℤ, ℚ and ℝ; multiplicative inverses exist for nonzero elements of these systems.
Order properties such as trichotomy say that for real a,b exactly one of a < b, a = b or a > b holds.

sections.heading: Factors, GCF and LCM
bullets: Prime factorization expresses a positive integer as a product of primes. The greatest common factor uses common prime factors with the smallest exponents; the least common multiple uses all factors with the largest exponents.
For positive integers a,b: GCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = ab. Check calculations by verifying divisibility and this product relationship.

sections.heading: Mathematical induction
bullets: To prove a statement P(n) for all integers n ≥ n₀, first prove the base case P(n₀).
Inductive step: assume P(k) is true for an arbitrary k ≥ n₀, then use that assumption to prove P(k+1). Clearly state the assumption and the target.
Conclude that P(n) holds for every n in the stated range. The base case alone or checking several examples is not a proof.
For a sum identity, write the expression through k+1 as the expression through k plus the next term, substitute the induction hypothesis, and simplify to the target formula.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: Classify each number in the smallest applicable set and explain why a decimal is rational or irrational.
When checking closure, find a counterexample if the operation does not stay inside the set.
In induction, label the base case, hypothesis, step, and final conclusion explicitly.

sections.heading: Rational numbers and decimals
bullets: A fraction a/b is in lowest terms when numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1 and b ≠ 0.
A rational number’s decimal expansion terminates if its reduced denominator has only prime factors 2 and/or 5; otherwise it repeats periodically.
To convert a repeating decimal to a fraction, let x equal the decimal, multiply by powers of 10 to align repeating blocks, subtract the equations to eliminate the recurring part, then reduce.

sections.heading: Complex-number arithmetic
bullets: Write z = a + bi with real part Re(z)=a and imaginary part Im(z)=b. The imaginary unit satisfies i²=−1, i³=−i and i⁴=1; powers repeat every four.
Add or subtract by combining real and imaginary parts. Multiply by distributing and replacing i² by −1.
The conjugate of a+bi is a−bi. The product of conjugates is a²+b², which is useful for division: multiply numerator and denominator by the denominator’s conjugate.
Modulus |z| = √(a²+b²); geometrically it is distance from the origin in the complex plane. Plot a+bi at coordinates (a,b).

sections.heading: Polar form, powers and roots
bullets: For nonzero z=a+bi, polar form is z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), with r=|z| and θ an argument satisfying cos θ=a/r and sin θ=b/r. Choose the quadrant from the signs of a and b.
Multiplication in polar form multiplies moduli and adds arguments; division divides moduli and subtracts arguments.
De Moivre’s formula: [r(cos θ+i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ+i sin nθ). It is used for powers and roots.
The n distinct nth roots of r(cos θ+i sin θ) have modulus r^(1/n) and arguments (θ+2πk)/n for k=0,1,…,n−1. List every k to obtain all roots.
Convert back to a+bi using cosine and sine; verify a root by raising it to the requested power.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: For complex division, show the conjugate multiplication and simplify to a+bi.
For polar conversion, report a valid argument and identify the quadrant; arguments can differ by 2π.
For nth roots, include all n angles and check that the roots are evenly spaced around a circle.

sections.heading: Ordered pairs and Cartesian products
bullets: An ordered pair (a,b) records a first and second coordinate; order matters, so (a,b) generally differs from (b,a).
The Cartesian product A×B is the set of all ordered pairs (a,b) with a∈A and b∈B. If A has m members and B has n, A×B has mn members.
A relation from A to B is any subset of A×B. Its domain is the set of first coordinates that occur and its range is the set of second coordinates; the codomain is the target set B.

sections.heading: What makes a relation a function
paragraphs: A function f:A→B assigns exactly one output in B to every input in A. An input cannot have two different outputs. Distinct inputs may share an output. The domain, codomain and rule together describe a function; its range may be smaller than its codomain.

sections.heading: Representations and tests
bullets: A function can be represented by ordered pairs, a table, a mapping diagram, a graph or a formula.

In a mapping diagram, every domain element must have exactly one arrow. On a graph, use the vertical-line test: any vertical line intersecting the graph more than once means it is not a function of x.
When a formula contains a denominator, require it to be nonzero; for an even root in real-valued functions, require the radicand to be nonnegative. These restrictions help determine the domain.

A one-to-one (injective) function maps different inputs to different outputs; a many-to-one function may map several inputs to one output. A function is onto its codomain when every codomain element is reached.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: From a relation set, list domain and range separately and check whether each domain value has one output.
State the domain restrictions before evaluating or composing formulas.
Do not confuse codomain with range or relation with function.

sections.heading: Operations and composition
bullets: For functions f and g, (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x), and (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x) where g(x)≠0.
Composition (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)): apply g first, then f. In general f∘g differs from g∘f.
The domain of f∘g contains x in the domain of g for which g(x) lies in the domain of f. Track these restrictions through the substitution.

sections.heading: One-to-one tests and inverse functions
bullets: A function has an inverse function on its full range exactly when it is one-to-one. Graphically, use the horizontal-line test.
To find f⁻¹: write y=f(x), solve for x in terms of y, interchange x and y, then state the inverse domain and range.
The graph of f⁻¹ reflects the graph of f across y=x. Check f(f⁻¹(x))=x and f⁻¹(f(x))=x on the appropriate domains.
If a function is not one-to-one, restrict its domain to an interval on which it is one-to-one before defining an inverse.

sections.heading: Polynomial and rational functions
bullets: A polynomial is a finite sum of powers with nonnegative integer exponents. Its degree is the largest exponent with a nonzero coefficient.
For a polynomial, zeros are x-values where f(x)=0. The factor theorem says (x−a) is a factor exactly when f(a)=0.
A rational function is a quotient of polynomials; its domain excludes values making the denominator zero, even if algebraic cancellation later removes that factor from the simplified expression.
Use factoring, polynomial division and the remainder/factor relationships to locate zeros and simplify expressions while preserving the original domain restrictions.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: For compositions, substitute carefully with parentheses and verify each domain condition.
When solving for an inverse, show the interchange step and test one composition identity.
For polynomial roots, connect each claimed zero with a factor and verify by substitution.

sections.heading: Coordinate plane and distance
bullets: A point is represented by ordered coordinates (x,y). The distance between P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂) is √[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²], from the Pythagorean theorem.
The midpoint is ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2). It divides a segment into two equal parts.
The slope of a nonvertical line through two points is m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁). A vertical line has undefined slope; a horizontal line has slope zero.

sections.heading: Equations of lines
bullets: Slope-intercept form: y=mx+b. Point-slope form: y−y₁=m(x−x₁). General form: Ax+By+C=0.
Parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is −1. A vertical line is perpendicular to a horizontal line.
For a line in general form Ax+By+C=0, its slope is −A/B when B≠0. If B=0 it is vertical.
To find an equation through a point, determine the required slope (or use two points), substitute into point-slope form, then simplify.

sections.heading: Circle equations
bullets: A circle with center (h,k) and radius r has equation (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r².
Convert a general quadratic equation for a circle to standard form by grouping x and y terms and completing the square.
A tangent at a point on a circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point. Use this with slope or distance relationships to find tangent lines or an unknown center.

sections.heading: Exam practice cues
bullets: Keep coordinate differences in consistent order in the slope and distance formulas.
For parallel or perpendicular tests, identify vertical and horizontal cases separately.
In completing the square, add the same value to both sides and verify the center and radius from standard form.

sections.heading: Parabola
bullets: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus and directrix. Standard vertical form (x−h)²=4p(y−k) has vertex (h,k), axis x=h and focus (h,k+p); horizontal form (y−k)²=4p(x−h) has focus (h+p,k).
The sign of p gives the opening direction; |p| is the vertex-to-focus distance. Identify which variable is squared before naming the axis and orientation.

sections.heading: Ellipse
bullets: An ellipse is the set of points for which the sum of distances to two foci is constant. For a horizontal major axis: (x−h)²/a²+(y−k)²/b²=1 with a>b; for a vertical major axis, the larger denominator is under the y-term.
Center is (h,k), vertices lie a units along the major axis, co-vertices b units along the minor axis, and c²=a²−b² gives the focal distance.

sections.heading: Hyperbola
bullets: A hyperbola is defined by a constant difference of distances to two foci. Horizontal standard form: (x−h)²/a²−(y−k)²/b²=1; vertical form reverses which term is positive.
The center is (h,k), vertices are a units along the transverse axis, and c²=a²+b². Asymptotes guide the branches: y−k=±(b/a)(x−h) for horizontal form; y−k=±(a/b)(x−h) for vertical form.

sections.heading: Recognizing and transforming conics
bullets: With no xy term, opposite signs on squared terms indicate a hyperbola; same positive squared terms with equal coefficients indicate a circle; same-sign unequal terms indicate an ellipse; one squared variable indicates a parabola.
Complete squares to find centers and standard forms. For a general quadratic with an xy term, the module uses coordinate rotation to remove the cross term before identifying the conic.
When sketching, mark center or vertex, axes, vertices, foci and asymptotes as applicable; label orientation and use scale consistently.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Memorize the defining standard forms and identify orientation from the squared terms and signs.
Show the algebra that converts a general equation to standard form before reading geometric features.
Check computed focal distances with c²=a²−b² for ellipses and c²=a²+b² for hyperbolas.
For line and conic problems, state what each parameter represents and verify the final equation by substitution when possible.
